cit.q: seeing that the post in the noisy [elephant] stable has been ruined...

note.p: A borrowing from Sanskrit śālā 'hall, house, shed' (Monier-Williams 1899, p. 1067), denoting a shed or hall attached to a household. This is probably its earliest Tamil attestation, and the only one in first-millennium texts in which it means a stable.This may reflect a concept borrowed from the north: the śālāstambha 'house-post' (MW), the equivalent of what we read in Puṟanāṉūṟu 220.3–4, where ālai veḷil may refer to the same structural element of the building.

The term śālāstambha already appears in Vedic manuals such as the Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra 7.1.30 (Ranade 1978, p. 216) as a 'pillar-post' in the eastern part of the sacrificial hall, but later more specifically in the context of stables.

An early example is found in Kālidāsa's Raghuvaṃśa (5th century CE) 16.41, which mentions elephants 'standing at the posts in the stables' (śālāgṛhastambhagataiś ca nāgaiḥ; The Lineage of the Raghus, p. 397). Here śālā clearly denotes the stable and stambha the hitching post. It is worth noting that the commentator AruṇagirināthaI am grateful to Csaba Dezső for drawing my attention to Aruṇagirinātha’s commentary. regards gṛha as redundant (śālāgṛham iti śiṃśapāvṛkṣavat), and thus interprets it as śālāstambha (Prakāśikā on 16.41; Achyuta Poduval and Raman Nambiar 1959, p. 337).

The South Indian Kāmikāgama (46.7–9; ca. 12th century CE) also describes the śālāstambhāḥ (in the plural) as 'stable-posts' for the elephant stable (śālāstambhā gajasya), while in the fifteenth-century treatise on elephantology, the Mātaṅgalīlā of Nīlakaṇṭha (11.8; Gaṇapati Śāstrī 1910, p. 29), śālāstambhapraveśa, 'entering between the stable-posts', is listed among the daily routines of elephants. Here, the term praveśa may refer both to going to the posts and to being hitched to them.

Since the association of the śālāstambha with elephant stables is already attested in Kālidāsa, who is close in time to the Puṟanāṉūṟu, although somewhat later, it is quite possible that the term was already current as an architectural element of elephant stables at the time of the Puṟanāṉūṟu. In poem 220, because of the line break, I read ālai veḷil not as a compound but as the 'post' (veḷil) of the 'stable' (ālai), although it is likely a loanblend of śālāstambha: the post that broke noisily when the mahout's bull elephant unexpectedly left.

If such beliefs already existed at the time, one may even wonder whether the mahout's sadness was not also due to the fact that, when his elephant broke loose and shattered the post of the shed, he "recalled" the relevant warning of the Vāstuśāstra: śālāstambhasya vā nāśe bhāryā tasya vinaśyati '...or if the house-post is destroyed, his [i.e. the owner's] wife will perish' (Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra, chapter 43, verse 40).

cit.q: entiram cilaikkum tuñcāk kampalai / vicayam aṭūum pukai cūḻ ālaitoṟum / karumpiṉ tīm cāṟu virumpiṉir micaimiṉ

You, who desired [it], enjoy the sweet juice of the sugarcane of all the press-houses surrounded by smoke, where the jaggery is being boiled, where the clamour does not cease, and where the machines resound!
kārk karumpiṉ kamaḻ ālait / tī ...
the fire at the press-houses fragrant from dark sugarcanes
aṟai uṟṟ' / ālaikk' alamarum tīm kaḻaik karump'-ē
the sugarcane with sweet stalks, which whirl in the press-houses [for pressing] after being cut/being beaten (aṟai uṟṟu)
ālai-toṟum ñerēreṉak / kaḻai kaṇ uṭaikkum karumpiṉ ēttamum

the sounds of sugarcane that is rapidly crushed at [its] stalks in all the press-housesThe press-house is possibly compared to a rain cloud because it is dark (with smoke from the boiling), it roars (with the noise of crushing), and it is full of liquid (the sweet juice, like rain). that looked like rain clouds
... along with the smoke from the press-houses of boiling and crushing
ālai mali pukai pōy aṇṭar vāṉattai mūṭi …
the abundant smoke of the press-houses goes [up], covers the sky of the celestials
tēṉ amar poḻil koḷ ālai viṉai cennel tuṉṉi
being abundant in the work of the press-houses set among groves where bees dwell, and in superior/red paddy
cūḻnta ālaiyiṉ vem pukai pōy mukil tōyum ārūril
in Ārūr, where the hot smoke of the surrounding press-houses goes [up] and touches the clouds
ālaik karumpiṉ iṉ cāṟṟai …
the sweet juice of the sugarcane [meant] for the press-house
ālaik karumpiṉ teḷivē pōṟṟi
O clarified juice of the sugarcane [meant] for the press-house, praise [be to you]!
ālaip paṭu karumpiṉ cāṟu pōla / aṇṇikkum añcu eḻuttiṉ …
the five syllables (pañcākṣara), which taste sweet like the juice of sugarcane that has gone into the press-house
… matuvum pālum / ālaiyil pākum pōla …
… like honey, milk, and the molasses in the press-house …
Yacōtai with sweet speech like sugarcane for the press-house
O [you who are] like a long sugarcane for the press-house!
Lord of lovely Āli scented by the smoke rising everywhere from the [sugarcane] press-houses
Nānkūr that is fragrant from the smoke of the [sugarcane] press-houses in the fields where [the juice] boils up

note.p: As demonstrated, the sugarcane context is well attested. This usage has close parallels with Sanskrit and Pali terms for sugarcane-processing sheds, such as īkṣuśālā and yantraśālā in the Avadānaśataka (tale 41) and ucchusālā in Buddhaghosa's Atthasālinī. Cf. entiram)
The mediaeval commentaries on 19: 23, 260–262 and Maturaikkāñci 258 gloss ālai as 'press'. This probably reflects a later shift from the building to the device it housed.

The term becomes truly widespread in the works of the early mediaeval Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava bhakti poets, although its use in the sense of 'sugarcane press' is rather allusive. Where ālai appears among the plants of the paddy fields, it is best understood as the sugarcane itself; elsewhere it denotes the shed in which sugarcane was pressed, as confirmed by the passages that mention the smoke rising from the ālai and the work carried out there.

The word is also attested in an eleventh-century inscription on the walls of the Vīrattāṉēśvara shrine at Kīḻūr, near Tirukkōyilūr (South Indian Inscriptions, vol. 7, no. 863; p. 434 = A.R. No. 236 of 1902; digital edition: DHARMA, SII 7.863). Describing the surroundings, the text reads: veḷ pūm karump' iṭai tuṇittaratt' āṭṭ' oli ālai ayalatu 'in the vicinity of the shed [with] the grinding noise (āṭṭ' oli) [caused] by those who cut the white-flowered sugarcane in the middle.' Here, too, ālai denotes the building in which sugarcane was crushed, and the verb āṭṭu- 'to grind, crush' describes the process. For the same verb denoting the same process, cf. Nālaṭiyār 34.1: karump' āṭṭik kaṭṭi ciṟukālaik koṇṭār those who, having crushed the sugarcane, took the jaggery in good time/at dawn.

A thirteenth-century inscription of the Raṅganātha temple at Śrīraṅgam (South Indian Inscriptions, vol. 4, no. 511; pp. 147–148 = A.R. No. 64 of 1892; digital edition: DHARMA, SII 4.511) mentions the compound ālaikkarumpu that designates sugarcane grown specifically for crushing in the press-house, as distinct from other crops of the land.

cit.q: tuḷi taru cōlai ālai toḻil mēva vētam / eḻil āra veṉṟi aruḷum
granting victory while becoming full of the grace of the Vedas, desiring the work of sacrificial hall/the press-house [for Soma?] amid the dripping groves
ālai ār aḻal antaṇar ākuti
the fire oblation of the Brahmins with precious fires of the sacrifical halls
ālai cēr vēḷvi aḻittāṉ …
he who destroyed the sacrifice performed(?) in the sacrificial hall
ālai vēḷvi aṭaintu atu vēṭkil eṉ?
What [is the use] if one nears the sacrificial hall and performs sacrifices there?

note.p: In parts of the Tamil Śaiva bhakti corpus, mainly in Appar, a new sense appears: the poet, probably aware that ālai derives from Sanskrit śālā, applies it to the sacrificial hall (homaśālā, agniśālā). Because of the groves, the passage of Campantar could also refer to the sugarcane press-house. The mention of the Veda in the same line, however, suggests a play on both senses: the sacrificial hall, and the place where, in the Soma rituals, plants were actually pressed.

cit.q: paḷḷa nīr vāḷai pāytaru kaḻaṉip paṉi malarc cōlai cūḻ ālai
sugarcane that is surrounded by groves of dewy flowers in the paddy fields, where vāḷai fish leap in the water of the ditches
teṅku uyar cōlai cēr ālai cāli tiḷaikkum viḷai vayal cērum poykaip / paṅkayamaṅkai virumpum āvūr …
Āvūr, loved by the Lady of the Lotus, where the ponds adjoin ripened fields in which the paddy sways around sugarcane that adjoins the groves of tall coconut palms
ālai cūḻ kaḻaṉi nīḷ pati āmāttūr
the long village of Āmāttūr with paddy fields surrounded by sugarcane
ālai cēr taṇ kaḻaṉi … naṟavu uṇṭu
having drunk … the nectar in the cool paddy fields that adjoin the sugarcane
ālaiyam cilai vēḷ
[Kāma]vēḷ with a sugarcane bow

sense.note: In these passages, ālai may denote the sugarcane itself, through a place-for-product metonymy in which the name of the press-house is transferred to the plant processed there. The first step in this development was probably the expression ālaik karumpu 'sugarcane [meant] for the press-house', attested in the bhakti corpora, which may already have been the name of a particular variety and was later shortened to ālai by ellipsis of the head noun. The best example in support of this is found in the Tamil Kantapurāṇam (ca. 14th century; Zvelebil 1995, 299).
